title: The Knowledge Revival
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Robert Pondiscio reviews the open-access book Developing Curriculum for Deep Thinking: The Knowledge Revival, a collaboration among figures including Nuno Crato, John Hattie, Dylan Wiliam, and Paul Kirschner with a foreword by E.D. Hirsch. He argues that education slogans such as teach critical thinking, not facts, are as futile as the search for El Dorado, because skills like critical thinking and reading comprehension depend on domain-specific knowledge. He summarizes the book's practical principles, including activating prior knowledge, building background knowledge, specifying content and sequence, and using retrieval and spaced practice. He insists that rote memorization of isolated facts is not the goal, and ties the case to equity, since a common knowledge-rich curriculum ends the stratification of knowledge between advantaged and disadvantaged students. He ends by acknowledging that philosophical, political, and practical resistance, including questions of who decides what content, makes the prescription far harder than the case for it.
points: Critical thinking, problem solving, and reading comprehension are not general skills that transfer like riding a bicycle, but depend on domain knowledge.

The book's curriculum principles are coherence, clarity, specified content and sequence, big ideas, and evidence-based strategies like retrieval and spacing, which set aside the bunch-of-facts caricature.
Pondiscio frames a shared knowledge-rich curriculum as an equity measure, since offering different curricula to different students stratifies knowledge.
Resistance comes from teacher autonomy worries, student-centered philosophy, and curriculum politics, and the book concedes that deciding which content and who decides is hard.
Leaving curriculum to individual teachers or non-expert teams produces incoherence and low rigor while burdening teachers.
quotes: You want students to “think like a scientist” instead of studying science? You can’t. There is no “thinking like a historian” until or unless you know what the historian knows.

Deep, transferable learning depends on domain-specific knowledge, and thinking itself is inextricably linked to the content of thought. A robust foundation of knowledge is not merely the raw material for thought, it is the scaffolding that makes higher-order thinking possible.

Those of us who are converts to this vision of education owe an unpayable debt to E.D. Hirsch, Jr. who recognized and sounded the alarm decades ago over the limitations of skills-based approaches and the vital importance of building a strong foundation of shared knowledge.

Demands for “culturally relevant” curriculum would matter less than ending stratification of knowledge implicit in offering one kind of curriculum to advantaged students and a different, less effective kind to disadvantaged ones.

As the above list should make abundantly clear, (and in anticipation of the predictable “bunch o’ facts” critique inevitably vomited up by critics) rote memorization of isolated facts is not the goal. Rather, teachers should strive to cultivate deep understanding by helping students build interconnected networks of knowledge that empower them to think critically, solve problems, and make meaning of the world around them.

The case for a common, knowledge-rich curriculum is all but unassailable, but the prescription is easier said than done. It invariably runs up against resistance due to philosophical, political, and practical factors.

Such conflicts mostly convince “stakeholders” to avoid them at all costs, which contributes significantly to the vicious cycle of educational incoherence and low rigor that inevitably occurs when individual teachers, grade-level teams, or subject matter non-experts are put in charge of curriculum, whether they want the burden or not.
